Luke 24:44 is the risen Christ opening the scriptures; Alma 45:2 is a father asking his son whether he believed what he was told about the records. The shared string is the English for referring back to something one has said.

The catechetical exchange at 45:2-7 — 'Believest thou in Jesus Christ, which shall come?' / 'Yea, I believe … with all my heart' — reaches for the KJV's baptismal confession at Acts 8:37 ('If thou believest with all thine heart … I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God') and for John 11:26-27's 'Believest thou this? … Yea, Lord: I believe'. Both are already adjudicated in this book: Acts 8:37 at Alma 6:8 and Alma 15:6, John 11:26-27 at Alma 19:9. 'Believest thou' occurs in seventeen Book of Mormon verses, thirteen of them in Alma, so by chapter 45 it is the book's own interrogative and not a fresh borrowing. What is fresh at this scene is what follows the confession, and that row sits at Alma 45:8.

The coincidence is the ranker's, not the text's — 2 Kings 2:3 is the sons of the prophets telling Elisha the Lord will take his master away, and nothing of that reaches Helaman's promise to keep his father's commandments. 2 Kings 2:11 does bear on 45:19 and is recorded in that row's composite.

'Works of darkness' occurs in two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11, and neither is selected by anything at 45:12. Paul's is a metaphor of night and dawn with armour attached; Alma's is one item in a list of vices ('the works of darkness and lasciviousness, and all manner of iniquities') where the phrase is doing no metaphorical work at all.

The fourth generation is a blessing in the source and a term of destruction here. The generation-count Alma 45 is actually working from is Matthew 24:34's 'this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled', which belongs to the Olivet material adjudicated at 45:11.

'He also blessed the earth, for the righteous' sake' is a striking half-line and 'for the righteous' sake' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The idea — a land spared or preserved on account of the righteous who are in it — has one biblical home, Abraham's bargaining over Sodom ('If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes'), and the pairing of 45:15's blessing with 45:16's curse on the same land is Genesis 18's logic applied in both directions. But there is no wording to test, and the Book of Mormon's own land-blessing-and-cursing doctrine is established from 2 Nephi 1:7 onward without it. Recorded because a reader might reasonably reach for Genesis 18 here.
